_note: Our own entries for the codex: this game's story features that aren't book rules, explained plainly and marked as such.

entries.title: Standing
entries.text: How a faction feels about your squad, from Hostile to Allied. It's this game's way of remembering who you've helped or crossed. It changes who talks to you, how they greet you, and what a contact can offer when you Get Connected. It never changes a roll. You can see it on the sector map (M) for every world you've been to, and in the hub's side panel for the factions there.

entries.title: Bonds
entries.text: How the squad's pilots feel about each other, from Rivals to Inseparable, built from missions survived together, mourning, helping each other and drinking together. The book's own example of a rules effect is used: the GM may reward a new bond with +1 Accuracy on skill checks to help each other during the next mission (Core p.50). The Bonded talent's bondmate can only be replaced when the relationship has changed (Core p.90).

entries.title: Deals
entries.text: Some people offer a job in exchange for a favor: do it, and they give you a reserve for the next mission. Lose the job and the offer is withdrawn, but you can still try another way, such as Get Connected.

entries.title: Situations
entries.text: Each hub has a conflict between two sides. Over a few missions the situation escalates, twists and comes to a head. Every mission moves it on, whether you win or lose.

entries.title: Hub
entries.text: A town, base or station where the squad walks around on foot between missions: talk to people, take downtime actions, pick jobs from the board.

entries.title: Manna
entries.text: The universal currency outside the Core (Core p.10). Prices come up in conversation, but the rules don't track money (Core p.18): your License Level and licenses decide what gear you can field.

entries.title: Enemy commanders
entries.text: Every enemy force has someone in charge: a named pilot with a personality, flying the toughest enemy on the field. They talk during the fight, and the ones who get away remember your squad and may come back for revenge on a later job. Their personality decides what they do when the fight turns: some surrender, some retreat, some offer a deal, and some fight to the end. Being the commander doesn't change their mech's stats.

entries.title: Talking terms
entries.text: The book says NPCs care about their own survival, surrender and retreat are perfectly good ways for a fight to end, and the GM can end a fight early once there's no question how it will turn out (Core p.60). So from the second round on, once half the enemy force is down (or their commander is badly hurt and a quarter of their force is down), you can call on them to stand down. Some commanders offer terms on their own, and some will offer to let your squad walk away if the fight is going badly for you. Accepting ends the battle there.

entries.title: Sector map
entries.text: The part of space your squad works in: a few star systems joined by blink gates, each with a few worlds, moons or stations. Each world has its own culture, landscape and hub, and its own situation. The map shows where you are, where you've been, the jobs and situation there, and how each world's factions feel about you. Open it with M in a hub. The map is this game's own feature; the setting's blink gates are from the book (Core p.10).

entries.title: Travel
entries.text: Between missions the squad can move to another world on the map, mechs and all. Inside a system that's a short flight; between systems it's a trip through a blink gate, which the book describes as fast and safe (Core p.10). Travel is part of the story: there's no cost and no travel time to track. Every world you leave keeps its people, jobs and situation for when you come back.
